issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may assess evidence concerning an acquitted co-accused when deciding an appeal by convicted co-accused, but may not set aside the acquittal in the absence of an appeal against it.
material_facts: One person tried jointly with the appellants was acquitted because the trial court considered the case against him doubtful.
No appeal was filed against that acquittal.
The appellants argued on appeal that the prosecution witnesses were unreliable because the trial court had not accepted their evidence against the acquitted person.
The High Court considered the evidence concerning the acquitted person while deciding the appellants’ appeal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to consider the evidence concerning the acquitted person incidentally when assessing the case against the appellants; it could not, however, formally set aside the acquittal without an appeal against it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 423(1)(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 permits reversal of an acquittal when an appeal against that acquittal has been preferred, but does not bar incidental consideration of evidence concerning an acquitted co-accused when resolving an appeal by convicted co-accused. The finality principle in Pritam Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1956 SC 415, concerns reopening an acquittal in subsequent proceedings and does not prevent such incidental assessment. The King v. Plummer, (1902) 2 K.B.D. 339, was distinguished because the acquittal there affected the logical basis of a joint-conspiracy conviction; that reasoning did not undermine the prosecution case against the remaining accused here. Bimbadhar Pradhan v. State of Orissa, (1956) SCR 206, supports the permissibility of incidental conclusions about evidence against acquitted persons in appeals by co-accused.

predicates.coaccused_appeal_without_acquittal_appea: A convicted person appeals after a joint trial, while no appeal is brought against a co-accused’s acquittal.
predicates.evidence_about_acquitted_person_relevant: A ground raised in the convicted person’s appeal requires assessment of evidence that also concerns the acquitted co-accused.

issues.definition: When a convicted person’s appeal requires assessment of evidence concerning an acquitted co-accused, the appellate court may assess that evidence incidentally but may not reverse the acquittal without an appeal against it.

issues.legal_issue: Common intention to commit murder may arise during an encounter, and a person who initiates an assault may share that intention with an armed companion who follows up the attack.
material_facts: The court found that the meeting between the two groups was probably accidental and that the prosecution had not established a prearranged plan to attack the victims.
One accused initiated the violence by attempting to assault a victim and continued the attack despite knowing that his son was armed with a gun and was behind him.
The armed son fired at the victims and pursued and shot one of them.
The court found that the common intention to murder developed after the encounter began, between the person who initiated the assault and the armed companion who followed it up.
The accused argued that the armed son had acted in private defence, but the court found that the other side had not initiated the violence.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a prearranged plan did not prevent a finding that common intention developed during the occurrence; the court sustained the murder convictions of the initiator and the armed companion, and rejected the claim that the companion acted in private defence.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 34 read with section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, common intention may develop at the scene and need not exist as a preconcerted plan before the encounter. The court inferred common intention from the initiator’s deliberate assault, his knowledge that the armed companion was behind him, and the companion’s subsequent use of the gun. Because the initiator was the aggressor, the companion could not rely on private defence on the facts found.

rule.if: joint_liability_murder_appeal and initial_aggression_by_one_participant and aggressor_knew_companion_was_armed and armed_companion_followed_up_attack

predicates.joint_liability_murder_appeal: The case is an appeal from murder convictions based on alleged shared criminal intention.
predicates.initial_aggression_by_one_participant: One participant initiated the violence by attacking or attempting to attack a victim.
predicates.aggressor_knew_companion_was_armed: The participant who initiated the violence knew that a companion behind him was armed.
predicates.armed_companion_followed_up_attack: The armed companion subsequently used the weapon against the victims, continuing the violence initiated by the first participant.

issues.definition: When a murder appeal based on shared intention involves an initial aggressor who knows that an armed companion is behind him and that companion follows up the attack, the murder convictions for shared intention may be sustained even if the intention arose during the occurrence.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for murder based on shared intention cannot stand where the evidence does not reliably establish the accused’s participation beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The accused was alleged to have struck one victim and injured a witness.
The prosecution witnesses did not mention the alleged attack on the victim until their testimony at trial, despite giving detailed accounts of the incident.
The evidence about the alleged injury to the witness was not satisfactory, and that injury was outside the charged common intention and was not the subject of a separate charge.
The court was not satisfied that the evidence safely established that the accused was present and participated in an attack from which a shared intention to murder could be inferred.
issues.conclusion: The case against the accused was not established beyond reasonable doubt; his conviction and sentence were set aside, and he was acquitted and discharged.
issues.legal_principle: A conviction under sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of the accused’s participation and the shared intention necessary to impose joint liability. Material omissions in detailed earlier accounts and unsatisfactory evidence of the alleged participation may leave reasonable doubt, entitling the accused to its benefit.

predicates.joint_liability_murder_appeal: The case is an appeal from a murder conviction based on alleged shared criminal intention.
predicates.key_alleged_attack_omitted_from_earlier_: Witnesses who gave detailed earlier accounts did not mention a material attack attributed to the accused until trial.
predicates.other_participation_evidence_unsatisfact: Other evidence offered to show the accused’s participation is unreliable or relates to conduct outside the charged shared intention.
predicates.no_reliable_evidence_establishes_partici: The remaining evidence does not reliably establish that the accused participated in the attack.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a joint-liability murder conviction reveals material omissions, unsatisfactory supporting evidence, and no reliable proof of the accused’s participation, the conviction must be set aside and the accused acquitted on reasonable doubt.

issues.legal_issue: An incriminating circumstance should not be relied on significantly against an accused when it was not put to the accused for explanation during examination under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on the accused’s having retrieved a gun from police custody shortly before the incident as support for a prearranged plan.
The circumstance was not put to the accused when he was examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
The court also noted that carrying a licensed gun in the area was not unusual.
issues.conclusion: It would not be fair to press the gun-retrieval circumstance significantly against the accused or to rely on it as support for a prearranged plan.
issues.legal_principle: Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 provides the accused an opportunity to explain incriminating circumstances. A circumstance not put to the accused for explanation should not be pressed significantly against him; its weight may also be limited where the conduct is not unusual in the relevant context.

predicates.criminal_trial_appeal: The case is an appeal arising from a criminal trial.
predicates.incriminating_circumstance_not_put_to_ac: The prosecution relies on a circumstance against the accused, but the circumstance was not put to the accused for an explanation during the trial.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal concerns an incriminating circumstance that was not put to the accused for explanation, that circumstance should not be relied on significantly against the accused.
